theOneRealDesignDecision.question: CP1 measured five shipped .pop-group instances and they are not uniform. Groups 1, 2 and 4 carry ONE trailing basis for the whole group; groups 3 and 5 carry a basis per entry. No single API renders all five byte-for-byte, so one of the two forms had to give.
optionsConsidered: PopGroup requires `basis`, rendered trailing. Renders groups 1, 2 and 4 exactly. Makes groups 3 and 5 unrepresentable, because they carry no trailing group basis and this would force a second one onto every group that already states its reasons row by row.
PopItem requires its own reason, rendered as a sibling. Renders groups 3 and 5 exactly. Makes group 2 render three basis lines where the product renders one.
Both optional. Renders every form, and enforces nothing, which loses the only rule this family carries.
theOneRealDesignDecision.chosen: PopGroup's `basis` is OPTIONAL and trailing. PopItem's `unavailable` is the reason and carries the requirement.
theOneRealDesignDecision.why: the rule the product states is about a CONTROL, not about a container. shell.css at .pop-item[disabled]: 'An unavailable entry reads as unavailable rather than merely unresponsive. Its reason is the .basis line its group carries, filled from the server.' index.html above the block: 'a control that has not yet heard from the server must not look available.' Putting the requirement on the group would have enforced a rule about where a sentence sits; putting it on the item enforces the rule the product actually wrote.
theOneRealDesignDecision.howItIsEnforced: there is NO `disabled` prop. `disabled` is removed from the prop bag with Omit<ButtonBase, "disabled">, and `unavailable` is not a flag: it IS the basis text. So an entry cannot be greyed out without saying why, because there is no prop that greys it out. Same technique as ModelCite's Omit<AnchorBase, "children"> at G-88, which is the established idiom in this package rather than a new one.
theOneRealDesignDecision.whatItCost: group 2 of the shipped account menu (three unavailable entries sharing one trailing basis) renders as three basis lines in the kit rather than one. Named as a deliberate divergence, not an oversight. Both forms remain composable: `<PopGroup basis=...>` with plain PopItems produces the shared-basis shape, and it is the shape the gallery's PopGroup entry shows first. What is NOT composable is an unavailable entry with no reason anywhere, which is the point.
theOneRealDesignDecision.whatWasNotDone: no `Meter`-style hard ban and no runtime children inspection. A React component cannot type-check what its siblings render, so a rule of the form 'this group must contain a basis somewhere' is not enforceable at the type and would have had to be a review comment. DEV_PROCESS rule 0 says a control that depends on someone remembering is not a control, so it was not written.

componentsWritten.home: src/shell.tsx, a new `top-bar menus` section between the frame and navigation sections. They are shell chrome, so they live with the shell rather than in a new module.
componentsWritten.TopMenu: <div class="topmenu">. No open state and no trigger slot: a trigger prop would have made this a menu widget with opinions about focus, keyboard handling and dismissal, none of which is a class this stylesheet ships.
componentsWritten.Pop: <div class="panel pop" role="group" aria-label={label} hidden={!open}>. The pair is emitted, not offered as a composition, because .pop declares no border, background or radius and a bare .pop renders as an unframed floating block. `label` is required: both shipped instances carry role=group plus an aria-label. `open` defaults to CLOSED, which is both the third law's quiet default and the state the product's static document ships.

instrumentWidened.what: test/_markup.mjs gained referencePage().shapeAtRevealed(selector), which skips the hidden test on the SELECTED element only.
instrumentWidened.why: the product ships both popovers hidden and the normalizer drops hidden elements, so a .pop parity case under the plain rule compares an empty string against an empty string. Green forever, unable to fail for the right reason: DEV_PROCESS 2.2.
instrumentWidened.whyItCannotGoVacuouslyGreen: reveal does not propagate to descendants, so the hidden feedback form inside the account menu stays dropped. And the KIT side of the case renders the panel open, so it emits no hidden attribute and its shape is never empty — a bug that made shapeAtRevealed return "" turns the case RED, not green. Both failure directions are red.
instrumentWidened.contractStatedWhereItIsRead: the widening is written into the normalization-contract header at the top of test/_markup.mjs, not only at the function, because that header is the list a reader checks before trusting a parity result.
instrumentWidened.gateAlreadyProvenAbleToFire: the markup-parity gate has an existing prove:gates injection (a component adding a wrapper the product does not have, needle 'Pill matches'). Adding cases to an already-proven gate does not require a new injection per case, which is how the other fifteen CASES entries already work.

whatIsNOTParityCovered.why: stated rather than omitted. An absent claim and an inapplicable one must not look the same.
whatIsNOTParityCovered.popOpenState: no case compares an OPEN popover against a shipped open popover, because the product has none: app.js opens them at runtime and index.html ships both closed. The revealed case compares the closed panel's content, which is the whole shape the static document carries.
whatIsNOTParityCovered.popItemAvailableArm: all seven shipped .pop-item instances are unavailable. The available arm has no product counterpart and therefore no parity case; it is drawn from the same rule read the other way and is named in its gallery `from` string in words rather than pointing at a screen that does not exist.
whatIsNOTParityCovered.themeToggleLabel: the shipped theme toggle carries <span id="theme-toggle-label">, a span with an id and NO class. The composed screen renders a plain <span> to match. That is a consumer element, not a kit component, and it is why the composed bar has one raw span in it.
